meta.title: Directive 2012/13/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 May 2012 on the right to information in criminal proceedings

items.text: This Directive lays down rules concerning the right to information of suspects or accused persons, relating to their rights in criminal proceedings and to the accusation against them. It also lays down rules concerning the right to information of persons subject to a European Arrest Warrant relating to their rights.
items.heading: Article 1
items.comment: The Act on Strengthening the Procedural Rights of Defendants in Criminal Proceedings (Gesetz zur Stärkung der Verfahrensrechte von Beschuldigten im Strafverfahren) was issued to implement the Directives 2010/64 and 2012/13 into the German CCP and CCA and entered into effect on 6th July 2013. The legislator has predominantly refrained from a literal implementation of the obligation to inform the suspected person of his/her respective rights as laid down in the Directive, since, in his opinion, from his assessment, the current law already largely complied with the requirements. Instead he has mainly opted for an addition to the wording of already existing provisions.

items.heading: Article 2

items.text: 1. This Directive applies from the time persons are made aware by the competent authorities of a Member State that they are suspected or accused of having committed a criminal offence until the conclusion of the proceedings, which is understood to mean the final determination of the question whether the suspect or accused person has committed the criminal offence, including, where applicable, sentencing and the resolution of any appeal.
items.comment:
The obligation to provide information in accordance with the guarantees of the Directive are tied to the status of a 'Beschuldigter', who in German criminal procedure is a person initially suspected of a crime, against whom the law enforcement authorities are conducting an investigation. The fulfilment of these prerequisites therefore indicates the earliest time of protection.

As the individual articles of the Directive name more specific time points for the instructions to be given according to them, the temporal scope of the respective guarantees is discussed in their context.

items.text: 2. Where the law of a Member State provides for the imposition of a sanction regarding minor offences by an authority other than a court having jurisdiction in criminal matters, and the imposition of such a sanction may be appealed to such a court, this Directive shall apply only to the proceedings before that court, following such an appeal.

provisions.comment:
The Administrative Offences Act does not contain any explicit guarantee of the rights contained in the Directive. Instead, by way of a general reference, the provisions of the CCP are declared to be applicable mutatis mutandis.

This implementation does not appear to be sufficiently clear and precise. This is particularly the case for the limitation to a corresponding application. This becomes clear, for example, with regard to the question of whether the omission of the information about the rights to remain silent and to consult the defence counsel leads to an exclusion of a following statement as evidence. The competent courts have often left the question open. For the adoption of an exclusion of the statements as evidence now inter alia OLG Bamberg in its decision of 27 August 2018 - 2 Ss OWi 973/18 - has ruled in this sense.
provisions.textEn: (1) Unless otherwise provided by this Act, the provisions of general statutes concerning criminal proceedings, particularly those of the Code of Criminal Procedure, of the Courts Constitution Act and of the Youth Court Act, shall apply mutatis mutandis to the regulatory fining proceedings.

items.heading: Article 3
items.comment: Since the instruction required under Article 3 was mostly already prescribed by law, indirect/de facto implementation is assumed overall.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspects or accused persons are provided promptly with information concerning at least the following procedural rights, as they apply under national law, in order to allow for those rights to be exercised effectively:
items.comment:
I. Overview of the relevant legislation

The Code of Criminal Procedure stipulates that the suspected person must be informed of his rights for two different situations separately:

1. Section 136 CCP regulates the case of the first judicial 'Vernehmung' (interrogation) of a suspected person. A 'Vernehmung' is given if the interrogator confronts the accused in official capacity and requests information from him in this capacity (BGHSt 42, 139, 145). Since the interviewer must face the accused in an official capacity, interrogations by undercover officers are not 'Vernehmungen' within the meaning of the provision. It also does not include spontaneous statements made by the suspect without the investigating authorities' initiative as well as statements made by a person before he or she was considered a 'Beschuldigter' (suspect).

section 163a (3) CCP refers to the provision of section 136 CCP for questioning by the public prosecutor's office and Section 163a (4) CCP for questioning by the police. However, the suspect must be instructed again at a questioning by a judge, even if he has already been instructed at a questioning by the police or public prosecutor's office, as well as at the first questioning by the public prosecutor's office, even if he has already been instructed at a questioning by the police. This is to make him aware that the corresponding rights also apply to this (higher) authority. In addition, information may also be required again in the event of a hearing by the same authority, if there is a concern that the suspect is no longer aware of his rights due to the lapse of time, e.g. if the previous hearing took place several years ago (BGHSt 47, 172).

2. Section 114b CCP regulates the instruction of the arrested suspect. According to section 127b (4) CCP, the provision is already applicable to provisional arrests by police and public prosecutors.


II. Time of Information

With regard to the time of the interrogation, the law only stipulates in section 163a (I) 1 CCP: 'The accused shall be examined prior to conclusion of the investigations at the latest, unless the proceedings are terminated.' For the rest, the time of the hearing shall be at the strategic discretion of the prosecuting authorities. According to this, it is conceivable that the accused learns of the accusation, but only at the end of the investigations or when the investigations are terminated is the accused not informed at all.

Of course, a detention is only then carried out when the conditions according to section 112 et seqq. CCP are fulfilled. As a rule, this presupposes, under section 112 CCP, a strong suspicion of a crime, i.e. the high probability that the suspect has committed a criminal offence, a ground for arrest, namely flight, or the danger of flight or the danger of being obscured, as evidenced by concrete facts, and the proportionality of the detention. These conditions will often only be established in the course of the investigations.


This handling in practice, which also corresponds to the predominant view in the literature, might be in contradiction with Art. 6 (3) a ECHR, which also requires that the defendant be informed promptly, in a language which he understands and in detail, of the nature and cause of the accusation against him. This is because notification of the proceedings and the first hearing or detention of the suspect do not necessarily fall together. It is now generally accepted that the guarantees also apply in preliminary proceedings, as far as this is necessary to ensure a fair trial and inter alia Frister argues, that not only the preparation for the defence in the main trial, but already the defence in the investigative proceedings required the information according to Art. 6 (3) a ECHR (Frister, StV 1998, 159, 160). In German law, the ECHR has the rank of a simple law as does the Code of Criminal Procedure. However, according to general opinion, it must be taken into account in the interpretation of the higher-ranking Grundgesetz, the German constitution. One could therefore rightly argue that, at least with regard to the opening of the charge, a corresponding obligation of the investigating authorities follows either directly from Article 6 ECHR or from the Grundgesetz (Frister, StV 1998, 159; Kölbel, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 2, 2016, § 163a para. 14).


However, according to recitals 19 and 28, it is still sufficient, if the information is provided 'at the latest before the first official interview of the suspect or accused person by the police or by another competent authority'. Thus, under section 136 (1) CCP, German law provides that information is to be given at the latest date which is compatible with the Directive. Schuhr (in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 2, 2016, § 136 para. 12) on the other hand, derives from the Directive that the relevant information must be provided at the time of the first investigative act which notifies the suspected person of the investigations in progress against him.

items.text:
(a)

the right of access to a lawyer;

provisions.comment:
The law obliges the interrogator to inform the suspected person in his first interrogation about the right to consult with a lawyer, regardless of whether the accused person is aware of it, and, if he wishes so, to provide him with information to facilitate contact.

According to the legislative materials (BT-Drs. 18/9534, p. 22), the amendment in sentences 3 and 4 served to implement Directive 2013/48. In laying down the previous case law, the law also obliges the interrogator to communicate such information as will assist the accused who wishes to consult a defence lawyer, especially to refer any emergency legal services (for further details see commentary on Art. 3 (4) of directive 2013/48).


The law itself does not specify the consequences of omitting or incorrect instruction. According to case law, failure to inform the suspect of his right to consult with defence counsel according to section 136 (1) 2 alt. 2 CCP will generally lead to the exclusion of the statement made, at least as far as it contains incriminating contents (BGHSt 47, 172). However, the suspect's counsel or the suspect himself, if he has been informed of this by the court, must claim this at the hearing by objecting to the use of his statement. Exclusion is also ruled out if it is clear that the defendant knew his or her respective right. In addition, the error of instruction can be remedied if the accused is heard again and is instructed 'qualified'. This means that he must be informed not only that he can contact a defence lawyer, but also that his previous statement cannot be used as evidence (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 136 para 10c).

As far as can be seen, there has not yet been any case law on infringements of section 136 (1) 3, 4 CCP. However, the rules lay down a prior, corresponding case law of the highest courts. If these obligations recognised by case law were violated, the courts rejected a ban on exploitation (BGH NStZ 2006, 236; NStZ-RR 2006, 181). This is rightly criticised in the literature. This is because the defendant needs this knowledge in order to be able to exercise his right to consultation with the defence counsel. If this information is withheld from the accused, the possibility of consulting the defence counsel remains factually just as hidden from him as if he had not been informed about his corresponding right at all (Albrecht, ZStW 131 (2019), 97, 105).
provisions.textEn: 1 At the commencement of the first examination, the accused shall be informed [...]. 2 He shall be advised that the law grants him [...] the right, at any stage, even prior to his examination, to consult defence counsel of his choice. 3 If the accused wishes to consult defence counsel prior to his examination, he shall be provided with information which makes it easier for him to be able to contact such defence counsel. 4 Reference is thereby to be made to any emergency legal services which are available.

A prohibition of the use as evidence is not to be assumed, since the suspect must be informed (if necessary again) in the proper course of a questioning and thus prior to any possibly incriminating statment.

Section 136 (1) sentence 5 CCP obliges the interrogator to inform the suspected person that a public defender can be assigned to him by the court according to sections 140 (1), (2), 141, 142.


The law itself does not specify the consequences of omitting or incorrect instruction. According to case law, a failure to instruct accordingly will not automatically lead to a ban on the use of the statement as evidence; instead, this depended on the circumstances of the individual case, more precisely on a weighing up of the interests of the accused and the interest in the prosecution of the offence, which would be adversely affected by the failure to provide information (BGH NStZ 2018, 671). Parts of the literature, on the other hand, rightly argue for the assumption of a prohibition of the use of the statement as evidence if the conditions for the appointment of a public defender of rights were actually met; (Schuhr, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 1, 2014, § 136 para 63). Indeed, instructing the accused about the right to consult defence counsel is of no use to the accused who believes he cannot afford one.

Instead of informing the suspected person about his right to information, German law stipulates corresponding information immediately. For details see the comment on Art. 6.

As stated in the commentary on Art. 3 (1), the information takes place at the first hearing or after detention and therefore not necessarily immediately upon notification that the person is suspected or accused of having committed a criminal offence. It is questionable whether this practice meets the requirements of Art. 6 ECHR.

It must therefore be assessed in accordance with the general principles of the case law whether it would adopt a prohibition of the use as evidence. Considering that the translation enables the suspect without sufficient command of the German language to understand the necessary instructions, one will have to attach the same importance to the instruction about the corresponding right as to the instruction about the right to remain silent or to consult defence counsel. With this reasoning, a prohibition of exploitation of the statement as evidence can be assumed, which can alternatively be justified by the lack of a comprehensible instruction about the right to remain silent, etc.

1A copy of the warrant of arrest shall be handed over to the accused at the time of his arrest; if he does not have a sufficient command of the German language, he shall additionally be provided with a translation in a language he understands. 2 If it is not possible for a copy and, where necessary, a translation to be handed over to him, he must be informed without delay, in a language he understands, of the grounds for his arrest and the accusations levied against him. 3 In that case, the copy of the warrant of arrest and, where necessary, a translation shall subsequently be handed over to him without delay.

Instruction of arrested accused

1The arrested accused shall be instructed as to his rights without delay and in writing in a language he understands. 2 If written instruction is clearly insufficient, oral instruction shall also be given. 3 The same procedure shall apply accordingly if it is not possible to give instruction in writing; written instruction shall, however, be given subsequently insofar as this can reasonably be done.

items.comment:
The Code of Criminal Procedure contains more detailed provisions on the modalities of the information only for the situation of arrest in section 114, 114b, as is also provided for in Art. 4 of the Directive. In contrast, the provisions on information at the beginning of the hearing only regulate their content.

The Bundesgerichtshof (Federal Court of Justice) as the highest criminal court, recommends that the instruction be based on the wording of the provision. However, this would be not compulsory; instead it would be sufficient for the instruction to clearly clarify to the accused his right to make a statement and to rule out any misconception in this regard (BGHR StPO § 136 Belehrung 17 (Gründe)). As far as can be seen, there is no further, more detailed case law regarding more specific requirements on the comprehensibility of the instruction.

items.subHeading: Letter of Rights in European Arrest Warrant proceedings

items.text: 1. nationalActs.title: Gesetz über die internationale Rechtshilfe in Strafsachen
nationalActs.titleEn: Act on International Cooperation in Criminal Matters

provisions.textEn:
Procedure following apprehension based on warrant of arrest pending extradition

(1) Upon their apprehension on the basis of a warrant of arrest pending extradition, persons pursued are to be brought before a judge at the nearest local court without delay, but no later than the day following their apprehension.

(2) The judge at the local court hears persons pursued about their personal circumstances, in particular nationality, without delay after they are brought before the court, but no later than the following day. The judge draws their attention to the right to avail themselves of the services of legal counsel (section 40) at any stage of the proceedings and to the fact that they are free to either make a statement or not make a statement regarding the offence of which they are accused. The judge then asks whether and, if so, for what reasons they wish to object to extradition, to the warrant of arrest pending extradition or to its enforcement. In the case under section 16 (1) no. 2, the hearing also encompasses the subject matter of the accusation; in all other cases, any information which persons pursued volunteer is to be placed on record.

Extradition documentation

(1) Extradition is only permissible if the documentation referred to in section 10 or a European Arrest Warrant has been transmitted which contains the following information:

1.  the identity of the person pursued as specified in the Annex to the European Arrest Warrant Framework Decision and that person’s nationality,

2.  the name and address of the issuing judicial authority,

3.  whether an enforceable judgment, arrest warrant or another enforceable judicial decision with the same legal effect has been received,

4.  the nature and legal assessment of the criminal offence, including the statutory provisions,

5.  a description of the circumstances of the commission of the criminal offence, including the time and place of commission and the person sought’s involvement in the offence and

6.  the maximum penalty provided for by law for the criminal offence concerned in the issuing Member State or, in the event of a final judgment having been given, the penalty imposed.

provisions.comment: As can be seen from the above provisions, the Act on International Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters provides for the person pursued to be informed of their right to remain silent and for defence counsel to be consulted after their arrest. The service of the EAW also informs the person concerned of the allegation in both factual and legal terms.
provisions.textEn: Persons pursued are to be informed without delay about their right to nominate legal counsel in the requesting Member State.

provisions.comment: Otherwise, the obligation to inform to the extent described above, in which the accused must also be informed in criminal proceedings, results from the reference in section 77 Act on International Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters to the provisions of the CCP and the CCA, among others.
provisions.textEn:
Application of other procedural rules

(1) In the absence of special procedural rules provided for under this Act, the provisions of the Courts Constitution Act and of the Introductory Act to the Courts Constitution Act (Einführungsgesetz zum Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz), of the Code of Criminal Procedure, of the Youth Courts Act, of the Fiscal Code (Abgabenordnung) and of the Act on Regulatory Offences (Gesetz über Ordnungswidrigkeiten) apply analogously.﻿

items.text: 2. The Letter of Rights shall be drafted in simple and accessible language. An indicative model Letter of Rights is set out in Annex II.

items.heading: Article 6
items.subHeading: Right to information about the accusation

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspects or accused persons are provided with information about the criminal act they are suspected or accused of having committed. That information shall be provided promptly and in such detail as is necessary to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings and the effective exercise of the rights of the defence.

provisions.textEn:
First examination

At the commencement of the first examination, the accused shall be informed of the offence with which he is charged and of the applicable criminal law provisions.

provisions.comment: While the judge and the public prosecutor's office must inform the accused at the beginning of the interrogation about the facts of the case and their legal assessment, in a police interrogation the interrogators only have to inform the accused about the facts of the case. This is in contradiction to Recital 28, which indicates, that the suspected person is to be informed about the possible legal classification of the alleged offence.
provisions.textEn:
Examination of accused

(3) The accused shall be obliged to appear before the public prosecution office if summoned. Sections 133 to 136a and section 168c (1) and (5) shall apply accordingly. [...]

(4) The accused shall be informed of the offence with which he is charged when he is first examined by police officers. In all other respects, section 136 (1) sentences 2 to 6 and (2) and (3) and section 136a shall apply to the examination of the accused by police officers. [...]

Warrant of arrest

﻿(1) Remand detention shall be imposed by the judge in a written warrant of arrest.

(2) The warrant of arrest shall indicate

1.  the accused,

2.  the offence of which he is strongly suspected, the time and place of its commission, the statutory elements of the offence and the penal provisions to be applied,

3.  the ground for arrest as well as

4.  the facts disclosing the strong suspicion of the offence and the ground for arrest, unless disclosure would endanger national security.

Issuance of warrant of arrest; translations

A copy of the warrant of arrest shall be handed over to the accused at the time of his arrest; if he does not have a sufficient command of the German language, he shall additionally be provided with a translation in a language he understands. If it is not possible for a copy and, where necessary, a translation to be handed over to him, he must be informed without delay, in a language he understands, of the grounds for his arrest and the accusations levied against him. In that case, the copy of the warrant of arrest and, where necessary, a translation shall subsequently be handed over to him without delay.

items.comment:
For the situation of arrest and provisional arrest, the exact scope of the information about the criminal act that the suspect is suspected of is laid down in the law: according to section 114b (2) CCP, the suspect must be informed about the offence of which he is strongly suspected, the time and place of its commission, the statutory elements of the offence and the penal provisions to be applied, the ground for arrest as well as the facts disclosing the strong suspicion of the offence and the ground for arrest, unless disclosure would endanger national security. He thus receives the comprehensive information, enabling him to exercise his rights of defence effectively.


For the situation of the first interrogation, which is more frequent in practice, a comparibly detailed regulation is lacking. Section 136 (1) 1 CCP requires the communication of the alleged 'Tat' - understood as the actual facts that may constitute an offence - and the relevant penal provisions. According to the case-law (BGH NStZ 2012, 581), the accused must at least be given a broad outline of the facts of which he is accused. The interrogator is granted a scope of assessment with regard to the details of the disclosure; he or she may therefore withhold details for reasons of investigative tactics. Also, details can only be disclosed in the course of the interrogation (Diemer, in: Karlsruher Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung, 8th ed. 2019, § 136 Rn. 8). In particular, it is disadvantageous for the exercise of the rights of defence that it is not recognised that the accused must also be informed of the evidence supporting the suspicion comprehensively.

It also appears to be not satisfactory that police interrogators are not obliged to disclose to the accused which criminal provisions are applicable (see commentary on Art. 6 (1), section 163a CCP). In the literature it is argued that for information according to Art. 6 (1) the factual classification was already sufficient, whereas the legal classification was only required by subsection 3, i.e. at the latest on submission of the merits of the accusation to a court (Quattrocolo, in: Ruggeri, Human Rights in European Criminal Law,2015, p. 81, 87; Allegrezza/Covolo, in: Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, p. 51 , 58). These requirements would be met by German law. However, according to its first sentence, Recital 28 is to be understood as a concretisation of Art. 6 (1) and in principle also requires a legal classification of the alleged offence. It allows to take into account the stage of the criminal proceedings when such a description is given, though. The reason for not obliging the police to inform the suspect of the legal classification of the crime is seen in the fact that police officers are not sufficiently legally trained to be able to establish a sufficiently reliable legal classification of the crime; an incorrect legal classification could even be detrimental to the interests of the defence. Thus it seems fair to assume that, as long as there is no reliable legal classification of the offence, the restriction of information duties of the police corresponds to the limits set out in Recital 28.



Regarding the time of the information, see the commentary on Art. 3 (1) and Art. 3 (1) c.


A clear incompatibility is apparent from the national legislation on penalty order proceedings, which have therefore already been the subject of several referrals to the ECJ. The penalty order may be the first opportunity for the accused to be informed of the accusation against him. Section 410 CCP grants him a two-week period to lodge an objection to the penalty order in order to defend himself against the accusation, to prevent it from becoming legally binding, and to bring about a regular hearing. Section 132 CCP obliges an accused person not residing in Germany to appoint a person authorised to accept service of a penalty order concerning him, with the period for lodging an objection against that order running from the service of that order on that authorised person. Thus, the period to file an objection would be reduced by the time needed by the appointed representative to transmit the penalty order to its addressee. If the order is received by the addressee after the expiration of the period for lodging am objection, it would become final and enforceable, even without the knowledge of the addressee.

As the ECJ has held in its judgments of 15/10/2015 in C-216/14 (Covaci) and of 22/03/2017 in C-124/16, C-188/16, C-213/16, 22/03/2017 (Tranca et al.), the relevant German law must therefore be interpreted in such a way that the addressee of the penalty order is entitled to the full period for lodging an objection from the date on which he receives the penalty order and, if necessary, is to be granted restitutio in integrum. In contrast to the otherwise higher requirements for a restitutio, the mere knowledge of the penalty order should suffice as a reason (cf. Wahl, eucrim 1/2017, 50). However, it follows from this approach that the penalty order would after expiry of the regular objection period initially become final and enforceable. In its judgment of 14/05/2020 - C-615/18 -, the Court therefore held that the Art. 6 precluded a legislation under which a person residing in another Member State, if he does not comply with an order imposing a driving ban on him from the date on which that order became final, is subject to a criminal penalty, even though that person had no knowledge of the existence of the order.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that suspects or accused persons who are arrested or detained are informed of the reasons for their arrest or detention, including the criminal act they are suspected or accused of having committed.

provisions.textEn:
Warrant of arrest

﻿(1) Remand detention shall be imposed by the judge in a written warrant of arrest.

(2) The warrant of arrest shall indicate

1.  the accused,

2.  the offence of which he is strongly suspected, the time and place of its commission, the statutory elements of the offence and the penal provisions to be applied,

3.  the ground for arrest as well as

4.  the facts disclosing the strong suspicion of the offence and the ground for arrest, unless disclosure would endanger national security.

Issuance of warrant of arrest; translations

A copy of the warrant of arrest shall be handed over to the accused at the time of his arrest; if he does not have a sufficient command of the German language, he shall additionally be provided with a translation in a language he understands. If it is not possible for a copy and, where necessary, a translation to be handed over to him, he must be informed without delay, in a language he understands, of the grounds for his arrest and the accusations levied against him. In that case, the copy of the warrant of arrest and, where necessary, a translation shall subsequently be handed over to him without delay.

items.comment: See the commentary on subsection 1.

items.text: 3. Member States shall ensure that, at the latest on submission of the merits of the accusation to a court, detailed information is provided on the accusation, including the nature and legal classification of the criminal offence, as well as the nature of participation by the accused person.

provisions.textEn:
First examination

At the commencement of the first examination, the accused shall be informed of the offence with which he is charged and of the applicable criminal law provisions.

Examination of accused

(1) The accused shall be examined prior to conclusion of the investigations at the latest, unless the proceedings are terminated. [...] In simple matters it shall be sufficient to give the accused the opportunity to respond in writing.

[...]

(3) The accused shall be obliged to appear before the public prosecution office if summoned. Sections 133 to 136a and section 168c (1) and (5) shall apply accordingly. [...]

(4) The accused shall be informed of the offence with which he is charged when he is first examined by police officers. In all other respects, section 136 (1) sentences 2 to 6 and (2) and (3) and section 136a shall apply to the examination of the accused by police officers. [...]

Content of bill of indictment

(1) The bill of indictment shall indicate the indicted accused, the offence with which he is charged, the time and place of its commission, its statutory elements and the criminal provisions which are to be applied (the charges). The evidence, the court before which the main hearing is to be held and defence counsel shall also be indicated. If witnesses are designated, their place of residence or whereabouts shall be indicated, whereby indication of the full address shall not be required. In the cases under section 68 (1) sentence 2 and (2) sentence 1, indicating the name of the witness shall be sufficient. If reference is made to a witness whose identity is not to be revealed either in full or in part, this fact shall be indicated; the same shall apply accordingly to the confidentiality of the witness’s place of residence or whereabouts.

(2) The bill of indictment shall also set out the relevant results of the investigations. This may be dispensed with if the charges are preferred before a criminal court judge.

Communication of bill of indictment

The presiding judge shall communicate the bill of indictment to the indicted accused and at the same time shall summon him to state, within a time limit to be set, whether he wants to apply for individual evidence to be taken before the decision to open main proceedings or whether he wants to raise objections to the opening of main proceedings.

items.comment:
Before the public prosecutor's office submits the bill of indictment including the accusation and its merits to the court, the accused has to be questioned according to section 163a CCP; in the course of this he has to be informed about the accusation to the extent described in the commentary on subsection (1). There is no provision for further information specifically before the charge transmitted.


The German legal situation thus proves to be insufficient for two reasons: Since police interrogators are not obliged to disclose to the accused which criminal provisions are applicable (see commentary on Art. 6 (1)) and since police interrogation is the rule (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, 62nd ed. 2019, § 163a Rn. 2), in the majority of cases the information on the legal qualification of the criminal offence is withheld from the suspect. Furthermore, it is neither laid down in the law nor recognised in case law to inform the accused about new factual findings or a change in the legal assessment (see commentary on (4)). It will only be provided (again) when the court submits the bill of indicment to the accused in accordance with section 201 CCP before deciding on opening the main proceedings. In this way, the defendant obtains comprehensive information at a time when he can still influence this decision and prepare his defence accordingly.


Relevant disadvantages compared to the notification at the same time as the merits of the accusation are submitted to the court, as required by the Directive, are not apparent: Even under the Directive, it is still sufficient for the information to be provided at a time when the defendant can no longer influence the decision to bring charges. Also under German law, it is sufficient for the information to be provided in time to allow the defendant to submit his defence before the court decides on the opening of the main proceedings. He must be given a reasonable period of at least one week for this purpose, which may be extended upon application or ex officio (Schneider, in: Karlsruher Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung, 8th ed. 2019, § 201 para 7). This should also ensure sufficient time to prepare for the main hearing, especially since the time delay compared with service by the public prosecutor's office should be slight, since the court must serve the charges without delay (KG StV 1994, 90; Wenske, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Band 2, 2016, § 201 para. 6).

Nevertheless, the information is provided after the point in time laid down in the Directive and therefore only partial implementation is assumed.

items.text: 4. Member States shall ensure that suspects or accused persons are informed promptly of any changes in the information given in accordance with this Article where this is necessary to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment:
A corresponding obligation to provide information about a change in the legal assessment is explicitly regulated only for the situation of the main hearing in section 265 CCP. For the investigative stage, this obligation is, as far as can be seen, neither prescribed by law nor recognised in case law.

In the literature, however, such an obligation is endorsed, to some extent with reference to the Directive (Schuhr, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Band 1, 2014 § 136 para 23 et seq.).

items.heading: Article 7
items.subHeading: Right of access to the materials of the case

items.text: 1. Where a person is arrested and detained at any stage of the criminal proceedings, Member States shall ensure that documents related to the specific case in the possession of the competent authorities which are essential to challenging effectively, in accordance with national law, the lawfulness of the arrest or detention, are made available to arrested persons or to their lawyers.

provisions.textEn:
Right to inspect files, right of inspection; accused’s right to information

(1) Defence counsel shall be authorised to inspect those files which are available to the court or which would have to be submitted to the court if charges were preferred as well as to view items of evidence in official custody.

(2) If the fact that the investigations have been concluded has not yet been recorded in the file, defence counsel may be refused inspection of the files or of individual parts of the files as well as the viewing of items of evidence in official custody insofar as this may jeopardise the purpose of the investigation. If the conditions of sentence 1 are met and if the accused is in remand detention or if, in the case of provisional arrest, this has been requested, information of relevance for the assessment of the lawfulness of such deprivation of liberty shall be made available to defence counsel in suitable form; to this extent, as a rule, inspection of the files shall be granted.

(3) At no stage of the proceedings may defence counsel be refused inspection of records drawn up of the examination of the accused or of such judicial investigatory acts to which defence counsel was or should have been admitted, nor may he be refused inspection of expert opinions.

(4) An accused who has no defence counsel shall be authorised, applying subsections (1) to (3) accordingly, to inspect the files and to view, under supervision, items of evidence in official custody insofar as the purpose of the investigation even in other criminal proceedings cannot be endangered thereby and the overriding interests of third parties meriting protection do not constitute an obstacle thereto.[...]

(6) If the reason for refusing inspection of the files has not already ceased to exist, the public prosecution office shall revoke the order no later than upon conclusion of the investigations. Defence counsel or an accused who has no defence counsel shall be notified as soon as he once again has the unrestricted right to inspect the files.

Obligation to clarify facts

(1) As soon as the public prosecution office obtains knowledge of a suspected offence, either through a report of an offence or by other means, it shall investigate the facts in order to decide whether public charges are to be preferred.

(2) The public prosecution office shall ascertain both incriminating and exonerating circumstances and shall ensure that evidence the loss of which is to be feared is taken.

(3) The public prosecution office shall also investigate those circumstances which are important for the determination of the legal consequences of the act. To that end, it may avail itself of the services of the court assistance agency.

items.comment:
Overview of the rules on the right to access the materials of the case

In accordance with the inquisitorial approach of German criminal procedure, the public prosecutor's office is obliged to start investigations and to investigate the facts of the case comprehensively, both incriminating and exonerating, provided there are sufficient factual indications to a prosecutable criminal offence, section 160 CCP. The results of these investigations are compiled in an investigation file. The criminal prosecution authorities are subject to an unwritten rule of the so-called completeness and truthfulness of the investigative files.

In contradiction to this, a praeter legem practised approach is to keep contents out of the files and thus to withhold them from the defendant due to promises of confidentiality to informants. These are only considered permissible in the area of serious crime. As a result, the identity of the informant and possibly the denunciation itself are not documented in the file (see Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 158 Rn. 16 ff.). Statutory exceptions cover information on undercover investigators (section 110b (3) 1, 3 CCP), findings from certain interception measures (section 101 (4) CCP) and information on witnesses at risk (section 2 (3) 2 of the Act on Harmonization of the Protection of Witnesses at Risk).

In all other cases, access to the file thus gives the suspect or defence counsel comprehensive access to the incriminating and exonerating investigation results of the law enforcement authorities.


The right of access to the investigative file and to view items of evidence is regulated in section 147 CCP. Subsections 1 to 3 concern the right of access to documents for the defence counsel. In principle, the defence counsel is entitled to inform the accused of the contents of the file (BGHSt 29, 99) and may hand over extracts, photocopies and the like to the accused to this extent. He may also inform him about imminent or already ordered investigative measures (OLG Hamburg StV 1991, 551), unless this serves the sole purpose of jeopardising the investigative purpose of an investigation or criminal proceedings.

Subsection 4 regulates the right of the undefended suspect to inspect the files and refers substantially to the provisions of subsection 1 to 3. The reason for this unusual structure is that the right of the undefended defendant to inspect the files was only established subsequently in 2018. Previously, only his right to obtain information and copies of the files on request was laid down, provided that this was necessary for an appropriate defence, that the purpose of the investigation, even in other criminal proceedings, was not compromised, and that there were no overriding interests of third parties worthy of protection. Subsection 4 is of practical relevance only if the accused is at liberty, because otherwise a defence counsel must be appointed for him according to section 140 (1) No. 4 CCP. Moreover, it may be a reason for the appointment of a defence counsel according to section 140 (2) CCP if only the defence counsel is allowed full access to the file (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62. Aufl. 2019, § 140 para. 27, 147 para 32; Beulke, in: Satzger/Schluckebier/Widmaier (eds.), StPO, 4th ed. 2020, § 147 para 48). If the appointment of a public defender of rights appears disproportionate in view of the accusation, the inspection of files must be granted according to Art. 6 (1) ECHR (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62. Aufl. 2019, § 147 para 32; on the legal situation before the introduction of section 147 (4): EGMR NStZ 1998, 429).


The general right of access to the file is laid down in subsection 1 for the defence counsel and in subsection 3 for the suspect. Subsection 2 1 contains the significant restriction that as long as the public prosecutor's office has not yet noted the conclusion of its investigations in the files, access to the files or individual parts of the files as well as the inspection of officially stored objects of evidence may be refused if this could compromise the purpose of the investigation. According to subsection 4 1, the right of the undefended suspect to inspect the files is subject to the further reservation that such inspection may not compromise the purpose of the investigation in other criminal proceedings and that it does not conflict with overriding interests of third parties worthy of protection.

Subsection 2 2 and Subsection 3 contain exceptions to the restriction of access to the file prior to the conclusion of the investigation under Subsection 2 1:

  • Where the suspect is in pre-trial detention or his provisional arrest has been applied for, information essential for the assessment of the legality of his detention shall be provided, normally by way of access to the file, subsection 2 2. The requirements of Art. 7(1) of the Directive on the right of the arrested and detained person to access the materials of the case are therefore satisfied.
  • In addition, access may not be denied to minutes of the accused's questioning and of such judicial acts of investigation in which the defence counsel has been or should have been allowed to be present, nor to the opinions of experts, subsection 3.

It also follows from the temporal limitation of the possibility of restriction under subsection 2 1 that, as from the moment when the conclusion of the investigation is noted and thus before the charge is brought, unrestricted access to the files must be granted.


If the public prosecutor's office refuses to grant access to the files, it must revoke this order when the reason ceases to exist, at the latest upon the conclusion of the investigations, subsection 6 1. According to subsection 6 2, the defence counsel or the undefended suspect shall be notified as soon as he has the unrestricted right to inspect the files.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that access is granted at least to all material evidence in the possession of the competent authorities, whether for or against suspects or accused persons, to those persons or their lawyers in order to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings and to prepare the defence.

provisions.textEn:
(1) Defence counsel shall be authorised to inspect those files which are available to the court or which would have to be submitted to the court if charges were preferred as well as to view items of evidence in official custody.

[...]

4) An accused who has no defence counsel shall be authorised, applying subsections (1) to (3) accordingly, to inspect the files and to view, under supervision, items of evidence in official custody insofar [...] If the files are not kept in electronic form, instead of granting inspection of the files, copies of the files may be made available to the accused.

items.comment: See commentary on Art. 7 (1)

items.text: 3. Without prejudice to paragraph 1, access to the materials referred to in paragraph 2 shall be granted in due time to allow the effective exercise of the rights of the defence and at the latest upon submission of the merits of the accusation to the judgment of a court. Where further material evidence comes into the possession of the competent authorities, access shall be granted to it in due time to allow for it to be considered.

provisions.comment:
At the latest when the conclusion of the investigations has been noted and thus before the charges are brought, the public prosecutor's office must in any case grant the defence counsel unrestricted access to the files on request. Prior to that date, his access to the file is to be granted insofar as this does not jeopardise the purpose of the investigation (see the commentary on Art. 7 (4)). German law therefore does not contain an explicit requirement to grant access to the file at the time when this is necessary to allow the effective exercise of the rights of the defence. In principle, however, this appears to be unproblematic insofar as access to the file is to be granted generally, unless the reasons for its restriction, which are to a large extent also laid down in the Directive, are given. Discrepancies arise only to the extent that German law permits further restrictions of the right of the undefended defendant to inspect the files in favour of private rights (see the commentary on Art. 7 (4)). As mentioned above in the commentary on Art. 7 (1), such a restriction of the right to inspect the files constitutes a reason to assign a public defender whose right to inspect the files is not subject to these additional restrictions. 


The obligation laid down in Article 7 (3) 2 of the Directive to grant the defendant and/or his counsel access to evidence obtained after access to the file has already been granted is not explicitly laid down by law. However, the right of access to the file may be exercised repeatedly without giving reasons. In addition, the Bundesgerichtshof (Federal Court of Justice) derives from the right to a fair trial according to Article 6 (1) ECHR in conjunction with section 147 CCP an obligation of the court of first instance inform the accused and his defence counsel when new investigation results are available in the main proceedings, thereby giving them the opportunity to take note of them (BGH NStZ 2006, 115, 116; NStZ 2017, 549).
provisions.textEn:
(1) Defence counsel shall be authorised to inspect those files which are available to the court or which would have to be submitted to the court if charges were preferred as well as to view items of evidence in official custody.

(2) If the fact that the investigations have been concluded has not yet been recorded in the file, defence counsel may be refused inspection of the files or of individual parts of the files as well as the viewing of items of evidence in official custody [...].

(4) An accused who has no defence counsel shall be authorised, applying subsections (1) to (3) accordingly, to inspect the files and to view, under supervision, items of evidence in official custody insofar [...]

items.comment: See commentary on Art. 7 (1)

items.text: 4. By way of derogation from paragraphs 2 and 3, provided that this does not prejudice the right to a fair trial, access to certain materials may be refused if such access may lead to a serious threat to the life or the fundamental rights of another person or if such refusal is strictly necessary to safeguard an important public interest, such as in cases where access could prejudice an ongoing investigation or seriously harm the national security of the Member State in which the criminal proceedings are instituted. Member States shall ensure that, in accordance with procedures in national law, a decision to refuse access to certain materials in accordance with this paragraph is taken by a judicial authority or is at least subject to judicial review.

provisions.comment:
The risk of a prejudice to an ongoing investigation is recognised as a reason to limit the right of access to the files of both the defence counsel and the undefended suspect, section 147 (2) 1, (4) 1 CCP. With regard to the right of the suspect, it follows from the wording of section 147 (4) 1 CCP that the risk of endangering investigations even in other criminal proceedings is sufficient. It would have to follow from the different wording of the restriction of the right of the defence counsel that in this respect only the jeopardising of the purpose of the investigation in the same proceedings would suffice. The Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has interpreted the relevant exception in the wider (BGH NStZ-RR 2012, 16). However, this decision dates from the time before the introduction of section 147 (4) 1 CCP; in view of the different wording, it is questionable whether the BGH can and will uphold this interpretation.


The risk of serious threat to the life or the fundamental rights of another person is a reason for limiting the suspect's right of access to the file. However, the corresponding reason for restriction in favour of private interests under German law is formulated more broadly by recognizing 'the overriding interests of third parties meriting protection.' High court rulings on interpretation have not yet been delivered. According to the will of the legislator (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 14/1484, p. 22), the protection of the privacy of third parties, the protection of at-risk witnesses as well as of company and business secrets should already suffice. At least the latter seems to go beyond the requirements of the protection of fundamental rights, which is why German law transposes the Directive only partially in that regard.
provisions.textEn:
(2) If the fact that the investigations have been concluded has not yet been recorded in the file, defence counsel may be refused inspection of the files or of individual parts of the files as well as the viewing of items of evidence in official custody insofar as this may jeopardise the purpose of the investigation. [...]

(4) An accused who has no defence counsel shall be authorised, applying subsections (1) to (3) accordingly, to inspect the files and to view, under supervision, items of evidence in official custody insofar as the purpose of the investigation even in other criminal proceedings cannot be endangered thereby and the overriding interests of third parties meriting protection do not constitute an obstacle thereto.[...]

provisions.comment:
As can be seen from the provision, the decision to grant access to files is taken

  • by the public prosecutor's office in the investigative stage of the proceedings and after the decision has become final and
  • by the main court during the intermediate proceedings on opening of main proceedings and in the main proceedings. 

In the latter case, therefore, the requirement for a decision by a judicial authority according to Art. 7 (4) 2 is satisfied.

An application for a court decision can be made against a negative decision by the public prosecutor's office, but only in three cases:

  • if the public prosecutor's office refuses to grant access to the files in contradiction to section 147 (2) 1, although it has already noted the conclusion of the investigation in the files
  • it refuses access contrary to subsection 3, or
  • the accused is not at large.

Thus, the restrictions of the right of access to documents specifically for the accused - endangering the purpose of the investigation even in other criminal proceedings or the overriding interests of third parties meriting protection - appear to be beyond judicial review. In this respect German law falls short of the requirements of the Directive (see also Mansdörfer/Schmitt, in: Allegrezza/Covolo (eds.), Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, p. 295, 310).
provisions.textEn: (5) The public prosecution office shall decide whether to grant inspection of the files in preparatory proceedings and after final conclusion of the proceedings; in all other cases, the presiding judge of the court seized of the case shall be competent to decide. If the public prosecution office refuses inspection of the files after noting the termination of the investigations in the file, if it refuses inspection pursuant to subsection (3) or if the accused is not at liberty, a decision by the court competent pursuant to section 162 may be applied for. Sections 297 to 300, 302, 306 to 309, 311a and 473a shall apply accordingly. These decisions shall be given without reasons if their disclosure might jeopardise the purpose of the investigation.

provisions.comment:
According to section 96 CCP, the highest official authority may block the use of files or other documents in official custody in criminal proceedings if the disclosure of the contents of these documents would be detrimental to the welfare of the Federal Government or a German state. According to section 110b (3) 3 CCP, such a blocking declaration may also be used to maintain the secrecy of identity of an undercover investigator, e.g. if there is reason to fear that revealing the identity would endanger the life, limb or liberty of the undercover investigator or of another person or would jeopardise the continued use of the undercover investigator.

The consequence of such a blocking declaration is that the otherwise existing obligation to submit files to the prosecution authorities is dispensed with and seizure of the files is inadmissible. In the normal course of proceedings, the blocking declaration therefore prevents the contents of the blocked documents from being included in the investigation file, but also from being used in criminal proceedings. The right of access to the file granted by the Directive is therefore not affected.
provisions.textEn:
Papers in official custody

The submission or surrender of files or other papers which are in the official custody of authorities or public officials may not be requested if their highest service authority declares that publication of the content of such files or papers would be detrimental to the welfare of the Federation or of one of the Länder. Sentence 1 shall apply accordingly to files and other papers held in the custody of a Member of the Bundestag or of a Land parliament or of an employee of a federal or Land parliamentary group if the authority responsible for granting authorisation to give testimony has made the relevant declaration.

provisions.comment: See commentary on section 96 CCP.
provisions.textEn: (3) The identity of the undercover investigator may be kept secret even after the operation has ended. The public prosecution office and the court responsible for the decision as to whether to consent to the use of the undercover investigator may require the identity to be revealed to them. In all other cases, maintaining the secrecy of identity in criminal proceedings shall be admissible pursuant to section 96, in particular if there is reason to fear that revealing the identity would endanger the life, limb or liberty of the undercover investigator or of another person or would jeopardise the continued use of the undercover investigator.

provisions.textEn: The decisions and measures taken in connection with witness protection shall be recorded. The files are kept by the witness protection service, are subject to secrecy and are not part of the investigation file.

items.comment:
See also commentary on Art. 7 (1)

German law German law makes differentiated use of the possibilities for restricting the right of access to the file which Article 7 (4) of the Directive allows.

The risk of endangering investigations and overriding interests of third parties meriting protection is recognised a ground to restrict access to the file (further deails below in the commentary on section 147 (2)-(4)). In addition and in accordance with recital 33 of the Directive, information on witness protection measures is not included in the investigation file, section 2 (3) 2 of the Act on Harmonization of the Protection of Witnesses at Risk.

The risk of a serious harm to the national security and partly the interest in the continued use of an undercover investigator is adressed by blocking the material in accordance with section 96 CCP, which is thus completely excluded from the criminal proceedings. The same applies to a risk for the life, limb or liberty of the undercover investigator or of another person and the public interest in the continued use of the undercover investigator according to section 110b (3) 1, 3 CCP (further deails below in the commentary on section 96 CCP).

Regarding restrictions due to promises of confidentiality see the commentary on Art. 7 (1)


What German law is missing, however, is the proviso that the retention of the materials must not curtail the righ to a fair trial. Such explicit reservations with regard to procedural fairness are generally not found in German law. In view of the fact that comprehensive inspection of files is to be granted at the latest when the charges are brought and that completely blocked evidence pursuant to section 96 CCP may not be used in the proceedings, it seems rare that a refusal to grant inspection of files in accordance with the provisions impairs the fairness of the proceedings. Nevertheless, especially with regard to the use on the identity of undercover investigators, this is a reason to assume only partial implementation.


With regard to the implementation of (4) 2, see commentary on section 147 (5) CCP.

items.text: 5. Access, as referred to in this Article, shall be provided free of charge.
items.comment: As recital 34 clarifies, Art. 7 (5) allows for provisions providing for fees to be paid for documents to be copied from the case file or for sending materials to the persons concerned or to their lawyer. These can be charged according to No. 9000, 9003 Kostenverzeichnis zum Gerichtskostengesetz (Court Costs Act - Schedule of Costs). The same applies to the fees for a printout of an electronic file or the transmission of a data carrier with the contents of an electronic file according to No. 9000 (4) Kostenverzeichnis zum Gerichtskostengesetz (Court Costs Act - Schedule of Costs). Apart from this, access to the file is granted free of charge.

items.heading: Article 8

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that when information is provided to suspects or accused persons in accordance with Articles 3 to 6 this is noted using the recording procedure specified in the law of the Member State concerned.

provisions.textEn:
Record of judicial investigatory acts

A record shall be made of each judicial investigatory act. [...]

Form of record of judicial investigatory acts

The record must indicate the place and date of the hearing as well as the names of the persons who were involved and participated and must state whether the essential procedural formalities were observed.

Record of investigating authoritiesʼ investigatory acts

(2) The examination of the accused, witnesses and experts shall be recorded pursuant to sections 168 and 168a insofar as this can be done without considerably delaying the investigations. If no record is made of the accused’s examination, the fact that his defence counsel participated in the examination shall be documented.

(3) The instruction of the accused prior to his examination pursuant to section 136 (1) and section 163a shall be documented. [...]

Instruction of arrested accused

The accused shall confirm in writing that he was given instruction; if he refuses, this shall be documented.

items.comment:
With regards to examinations, the requirement to note the aformentioned instructions arises from the general rules on the documentation of pre-trial hearings and the recording of the trial. Section 168, 168a CCP govern the recording of a judicial investigative act, to which the section 168b CCP on the recording of investigative acts by other investigating authorities refers. According to these, the essential formalities of the hearing must be recorded, which also include the instructions precribed by law (instead of many Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 168a GVG para. 2).


Section 114b (1) 4 CCP regulates the documentation of the instruction of the arrested suspect by generally requiring his written confirmation.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that suspects or accused persons or their lawyers have the right to challenge, in accordance with procedures in national law, the possible failure or refusal of the competent authorities to provide information in accordance with this Directive.

provisions.comment:
Against a refusal by the public prosecutor's office in the investigative stage, a decision by the court competent according to section 162 CCP may be applied for, section 147 (5) 2 CCP (see commentary on Art. 7(4)). A refusal by the court can be challenged with a complaint according to section 304 (1), (4) 2 No. 4 CCP. However, according to recent case-law, a refusal by the court hearing the case after the main proceedings have been opened cannot be challenged pursuant to section 305 1 CCP (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, 62nd ed. 2019, § 147 para 41 with further references).

In such cases, the refusal of access to the file may, in exceptional cases, justify an appeal on points of law according to section 333 et seqq CCP. A refusal by the adjudicating court can also establish a substantial limitation of the defence, which constitutes a so-called absolute ground of appeal pursuant to section 338 no. 8 CCP; it is then legally presumed that the judgment was based on a violation of the law. In other cases like the refusal by the prosecuting authorities, the restraint may continue to have effect in the main hearing and thus constitute a violation of law that the judgment is based on.

The possibilities of challeging the failure or refusal of the competent authorities to grant access to the materials of the case in accordance with this Directive itself are not fully exhaustive, but correspond to the possibilities possibilities for challeging comparable procedural errors. Since the contestability under national law is declared sufficient and, according to the recital 36, no specific appeal procedure, separate mechanism, or a complaint procedure needs to be installed, it is fair to assume full implementation.
provisions.textEn: 2 If the public prosecution office refuses inspection of the files after noting the termination of the investigations in the file, if it refuses inspection pursuant to subsection (3) or if the accused is not at liberty, a decision by the court competent pursuant to section 162 may be applied for. 3 Sections 297 to 300, 302, 306 to 309, 311a and 473a shall apply accordingly.

Admissibility

A complaint shall be admissible against all orders made by the courts of first instance or in proceedings on an appeal on points of fact and law and against directions given by the presiding judge, the judge in the preliminary investigation, and by a commissioned or a requested judge, unless such orders are expressly exempted from appellate remedy by law.

Procedure for seizure

The person concerned may at any time apply for a court decision.

Admissibility

An appeal on points of law shall be admissible against judgments of the criminal divisions, of the criminal divisions with lay judges and against judgments of the higher regional courts pronounced at first instance.

Grounds for appeal on points of law

(1) An appeal on points of law may be filed only on the ground that the judgment was based on a violation of the law.

(2) Failure to apply a legal norm or erroneous application of a legal norm shall constitute a violation of the law.

provisions.comment:
The accused may in principle challenge the manner of the judicial hearing by lodging a complaint pursuant to Sections 304 et seqq. CCP. However, by the time the complaint court decides on the complaint, the complaint will at the latest be outdated in procedural terms. According to the case-law, an complaint is thus inadmissible or without merit. This is criticised in the literature.

The manner of a public prosecutor's office or police interrogation can be challenged with an application for a court decision pursuant to section 98 (2) 2 CCP analogously (to this topic see Rogall, in: Systematischer Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung Band 2, 5. Aufl. 2016, § 136 para 76).


Of greater practical importance, however, is the objection of error of instruction with an appeal on points of law according to section 333 et seqq. CCP. Failures to instruct may have the consequence that subsequent incriminating statements made by the suspected person may not be used in further proceedings (for details, see the commentary on the individual obligations to instruct the suspected and arrested person above). If the recognising court disregards such a ban on exploitation, this may justify the appeal on points of law according to section 333 et seqq CCP. In principle, according to section 337 CCP an appeal will only be successful if the judgment is based on a violation of law, i.e. if there is at least the possibility that the outcome would have been different had the proceedings been free of errors of law. However, this is likely to be the case with the exploitation of any incriminating submission of the suspected person.


The possibilities of challeging the failure or refusal of the competent authorities to provide information in accordance with this Directive itself are not fully exhaustive, but correspond to the possibilities for challeging comparable procedural errors. Since the contestability under national law is declared sufficient and, according to the recital 36, no specific appeal procedure, separate mechanism, or a complaint procedure needs to be installed, it is fair to assume full implementation.

The sole purpose of this model is to assist national authorities in drawing up their Letter of Rights at national level. Member States are not bound to use this model. When preparing their Letter of Rights, Member States may amend this model in order to align it with their national rules and add further useful information. The Member State’s Letter of Rights must be given upon arrest or detention. This however does not prevent Member States from providing suspects or accused persons with written information in other situations during criminal proceedings.


A. ASSISTANCE OF A LAWYER/ENTITLEMENT TO LEGAL AID


You have the right to speak confidentially to a lawyer. A lawyer is independent from the police. Ask the police if you need help to get in contact with a lawyer, the police shall help you. In certain cases the assistance may be free of charge. Ask the police for more information.


B. INFORMATION ABOUT THE ACCUSATION


You have the right to know why you have been arrested or detained and what you are suspected or accused of having done.


C. INTERPRETATION AND TRANSLATION


If you do not speak or understand the language spoken by the police or other competent authorities, you have the right to be assisted by an interpreter, free of charge. The interpreter may help you to talk to your lawyer and must keep the content of that communication confidential. You have the right to translation of at least the relevant passages of essential documents, including any order by a judge allowing your arrest or keeping you in custody, any charge or indictment and any judgment. You may in some circumstances be provided with an oral translation or summary.


D. RIGHT TO REMAIN SILENT


While questioned by the police or other competent authorities, you do not have to answer questions about the alleged offence. Your lawyer can help you to decide on that.


E. ACCESS TO DOCUMENTS


When you are arrested and detained, you (or your lawyer) have the right to access essential documents you need to challenge the arrest or detention. If your case goes to court, you (or your lawyer) have the right to access the material evidence for or against you.


F. INFORMING SOMEONE ELSE ABOUT YOUR ARREST OR DETENTION/INFORMING YOUR CONSULATE OR EMBASSY


When you are arrested or detained, you should tell the police if you want someone to be informed of your detention, for example a family member or your employer. In certain cases the right to inform another person of your detention may be temporarily restricted. In such cases the police will inform you of this.


If you are a foreigner, tell the police if you want your consular authority or embassy to be informed of your detention. Please also tell the police if you want to contact an official of your consular authority or embassy.


G. URGENT MEDICAL ASSISTANCE


When you are arrested or detained, you have the right to urgent medical assistance. Please let the police know if you are in need of such assistance.


H. PERIOD OF DEPRIVATION OF LIBERTY


After your arrest you may be deprived of liberty or detained for a maximum period of … [fill in applicable number of hours/days]. At the end of that period you must either be released or be heard by a judge who will decide on your further detention. Ask your lawyer or the judge for information about the possibility to challenge your arrest, to review the detention or to ask for provisional release.

items.comment: German law does not provide for an explicit orientation of the federally organised public prosecutor's offices towards the attached Letter of Rights. However, the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection provides a template for the written instruction of detained persons in German as well as in several foreign languages (http://www.bmjv.de/SiteGlobals/Forms/Suche/Belehrungsformularesuche_Formular.html, as of 26.04.2020). Since German law obliges the prosecution authorities to give the arrested accused person the instructions provided for in the Directive in writing, it seems fair to assume a de facto implementation.

A. INFORMATION ABOUT THE EUROPEAN ARREST WARRANT


You have the right to be informed about the content of the European Arrest Warrant on the basis of which you have been arrested.


B. ASSISTANCE OF A LAWYER


You have the right to speak confidentially to a lawyer. A lawyer is independent from the police. Ask the police if you need help to get in contact with a lawyer, the police shall help you. In certain cases the assistance may be free of charge. Ask the police for more information.


C. INTERPRETATION AND TRANSLATION


If you do not speak or understand the language spoken by the police or other competent authorities, you have the right to be assisted by an interpreter, free of charge. The interpreter may help you to talk to your lawyer and must keep the content of that communication confidential. You have the right to a translation of the European Arrest Warrant in a language you understand. You may in some circumstances be provided with an oral translation or summary.


D. POSSIBILITY TO CONSENT


You may consent or not consent to being surrendered to the State seeking you. Your consent would speed up the proceedings. [Possible addition of certain Member States: It may be difficult or even impossible to change this decision at a later stage.] Ask the authorities or your lawyer for more information.


E. HEARING


If you do not consent to your surrender, you have the right to be heard by a judicial authority.
